entries.7f3a04e2c4684cefea0951c6f70e6bd58219a9f4: <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.19.27" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Matt.19.27" sID="gen100951" type="section"/> <div sID="gen100952" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.19.27">Matthew 19:27</reference>.</hi> <hi type="italic">Then Peter answering said to him.</hi> Peter tacitly compares himself and the other disciples to the <hi type="italic">rich </hi>man, whom the world had turned aside from Christ. As they had led a poor and wandering <note n="639"> <div sID="gen100953" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Et suiete a changer souvent de demeurance</foreign>;” — “and liable to change their residence frequently.”<div eID="gen100953" type="x-p"/> </note> life, which was not unaccompanied by disgrace and by annoyances, and as no better condition for the future presented itself, he properly inquires if it be to no purpose that they have <hi type="italic">left all </hi>their property, and devoted themselves to Christ; for it would be unreasonable if, after having been stripped of their property by the Lord, they should not be restored to a better condition.<div eID="gen100952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen100954" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Lo, we have left all.</hi> But what were those <hi type="italic">all things? </hi>for, being mean and very poor men, they scarcely had a home to leave, and therefore this boasting might appear to be ridiculous. And certainly experience shows how large an estimate men commonly form of their duties towards God, as at this day, among the Papists, those who were little else than beggars make it a subject of haughty reproach that they have sustained great damage for the sake of the Gospel. But the disciples may be excused on this ground, that, though their wealth was not magnificent, they subsisted at home, by their manual labors, not less cheerfully than the richest man. And we know that men of humble condition, who have been accustomed to a quiet and modest life, reckon it a greater hardship to be torn from their wives and children than those who are led by ambition, or who are carried in various directions by the gale of prosperity. Certainly, if some reward had not been reserved for the disciples, it would have been foolish in them to have changed their course of life. <note n="640"> <div sID="gen100955" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">D’avoir change d’estat et de facon de vivre</foreign>;” — “for having changed their condition and their way of living.”<div eID="gen100955" type="x-p"/> </note> But though on that ground they might be excused, they err in this respect, that they demand a triumph to be given them, before they have finished their warfare. If we ever experience such uneasiness at delay, and if we are tempted by impatience, let us learn first to reflect on the comforts by which the Lord soothes the bitterness of the cup in this world, and next elevate our minds to the hope of the heavenly life; for these two points embrace the answer of Christ.<div eID="gen100954" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.19.27" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen100951" osisID="Matt.19.27" type="section"/>
entries.ea7ca2d1059647552483bec924e72123d6fda06e: <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.19.28" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Matt.19.28" sID="gen100956" type="section"/> <div sID="gen100957" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">28.</hi> <hi type="italic">Verily I say to you.</hi> That the disciples may not think that they have lost their pains, and repent of having begun the course, Christ warns them that the glory of his kingdom, which at that time was still hidden, was about to be revealed. As if he had said, “There is no reason why that mean condition should discourage you; for I, who am scarcely equal to the lowest, will at length ascend to my throne of majesty. Endure then for a little, till the time arrive for revealing nay glory.” And what does he then promise to them? That they shall be partakers of the same glory.<div eID="gen100957" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen100958" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">You also shall sit on twelve thrones</hi> By assigning to them <hi type="italic">thrones</hi>, from which they may <hi type="italic">judge the twelve tribes of Israel, </hi>he compares them to assessors, or first councilors and judges, who occupy the highest seats in the royal council. We know that the number of those who were chosen to be apostles was <hi type="italic">twelve</hi>, in order to testify that, by the agency of Christ, God purposed to collect the remnant of his people which was scattered. This was a very high rank, but hitherto was concealed; and therefore Christ holds their wishes in suspense till the latest revelation of his kingdom, when they will fully receive the fruit of their election. And though the kingdom of Christ is, in some respects, manifested by the preaching of the Gospel, there is no doubt that Christ here speaks of the last day.<div eID="gen100958" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen100959" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">In the regeneration.</hi> Some connect this term with the following clause. In this sense, <hi type="italic">regeneration </hi>would be nothing else than the renovation which shall follow our restoration, when life shall swallow up what is mortal, and when our mean body shall be transformed into the heavenly glory of Christ. But I rather explain <hi type="italic">regeneration </hi>as referring to the first coming of Christ; for then the world began to be renewed, and arose out of the darkness of death into the light of life. And this way of speaking occurs frequently in the Prophets, and is exceedingly adapted to the connection of this passage. For the renovation of the Church, which had been so frequently promised, had raised an expectation of wonderful happiness, as soon as the Messiah should appear; and therefore, in order to guard against that error, Christ distinguishes between the beginning and the completion of his reign.<div eID="gen100959" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.19.28" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen100956" osisID="Matt.19.28" type="section"/>
entries.25c6b961d80ebd0de03986b1399e43157b82f9ae: <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.19.29" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Matt.19.29" sID="gen100964" type="section"/> <div sID="gen100965" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.19.29">Matthew 19:29</reference>.</hi> <hi type="italic">And whosoever shall forsake.</hi> After having raised the expectation of his followers to the hope of a future life, he supports them by immediate consolations, <note n="641"> <div sID="gen100966" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">De consolations de la vie presente</foreign>;” — “by consolations of the present life.”<div eID="gen100966" type="x-p"/> </note> and strengthens them for bearing the cross. For though God permit his people to be severely afflicted, he never abandons them, so as not to recompense their distresses by his assistance. And here he does not merely address the apostles, but takes occasion to direct his discourse generally to all the godly. The substance of it is this: Those who shall willingly <hi type="italic">lose all </hi>for the sake of Christ, will be more happy even in this life than if they had retained the full possession of them; but the chief reward is laid up for them in heaven.<div eID="gen100965" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen100967" type="x-p"/>But what he promises about recompensing them <hi type="italic">a hundredfold </hi>appears not at all to agree with experience; for in the greater number of cases, those who have been deprived of their parents, or children, and other relatives — who have been reduced to widowhood, and stripped of their wealth, for the testimony of Christ — are so far from recovering their property, that in exile, solitude and desertion, they have a hard struggle with severe poverty. I reply, if any man estimate aright the immediate grace of God, by which he relieves the sorrows of his people, he will acknowledge that it is justly preferred to all the riches of the world. For though <hi type="italic">unbelievers flourish, </hi>(<reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.92.7">Psalm 92:7</reference>,) yet as they <hi type="italic">know not what awaits them on the morro</hi>w (<reference osisRef="Bible:Jas.4.14">James 4:14</reference>,) they must be always tossed about in perplexity and terror, and it is only by stupefying themselves in some sort that they can at all enjoy prosperity. <note n="642"> <div sID="gen100968" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Ils ne peuvent iouir a leur aise des biens qu’ils ont, sinon qu’ils en-trent comme en une stupidite, et effacent tout sentiment de leur conscience</foreign>;” — “they cannot enjoy at their ease the good things which they possess, unless they become, as it were, stupid, and destroy every feeling of their conscience.”<div eID="gen100968" type="x-p"/> </note> Yet God gladdens his people, so that the small portion of good which they enjoy is more highly valued by them, and far sweeter, than if out of Christ they had enjoyed an unlimited abundance of good things. In this sense I interpret the expression used by Mark, <hi type="italic">with persecutions; </hi>as if Christ had said, Though <hi type="italic">persecutions </hi>always await the godly in this world, and though the cross, as it were, is attached to their back, yet so sweet is the seasoning of the grace of God, which gladdens them, that their condition is more desirable than the luxuries of kings.<div eID="gen100967" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.19.29" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen100964" osisID="Matt.19.29" type="section"/>

30. And many that are first shall be last. This sentence was added in order to shake off the indolence of the flesh. The apostles, though they had scarcely begun the course, were hastening to demand the prize. And such is the disposition of almost all of us, that, when a month has elapsed, we ask, like soldiers who have served their time, to receive a discharge. But Christ exhorts those who have begun well (Galatians 3:3; 5:7) to vigorous perseverance, and at the same time gives warning, that it will be of no avail to runners to have begun with alacrity, if they lose courage in the midst of the course. In like manner Paul also warns us, that not all who run obtain t/re prize, (1 Corinthians 9:24;) and in another passage he exhorts believers, by referring to his own example, to:
forget those things which are behind, and press forward to the remaining portion of their course, (Philippians 3:13,14.)
As often, therefore, as we call to mind the heavenly crown, we ought, as it were, to feel the application of fresh spurs, that we may not be more indolent for the future.

1. For the kingdom of heaven is like a householder, who went out at break of day to hire laborers into his vineyard. 2. And having made an agreement with the laborers for a penny a day, he sent them into his vineyard. 3. And having gone out about the third hour, he saw others standing idle in the market-place. 4. And he said to them, Go you also into the vineyard, and whatever shall be right I will give you. 5. And they went away. And again he went out about the sixth and ninth hour, and acted in the same manner. 6. And about the eleventh hour he went out, and found others standing idle, and said to them, Why stand you here all the day idle? 7. They say to him, Because nobody hath hired us. He saith to them, Go you also into the vineyard, and you will receive what shall be right. 8. And when the evening was come, the master of the vineyard saith to his steward, Call the laborers, and pay them their hire, beginning with the last even to the first. 9. And when they came who had come about the eleventh hour, they received every man a penny. 10. And they who had come first thought that they would receive more, and they also received every man a penny. 11. And when they had received it, they murmured against the householder, 12. Saying, These last have been but one hour at work, and thou hast made them equal to us, who have endured the burden of the day and the heat. 13. But he answering one of them, said, Friend, I do thee no wrong: didst not thou agree with me for a penny? 14. Take what is thine, and go away: and I intend to give to this last as much as to thee. 15. Is it not lawful for me to do what I will with my own property? Is thy eye evil, because I am good? 16. So the last shall be first, and the first shall be last: for many are called, but few are chosen.

                        </ns0:gap>em,</ns0:hi> yet was come into that <ns0:hi>Province,</ns0:hi> where the <ns0:hi>Pharisees</ns0:hi> had the greatest Power, and were in greater Numbers: Now they come to him, <ns0:hi>Tempting him,</ns0:hi> where the Word <ns0:hi>Tempting,</ns0:hi> ra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther signifies generally <ns0:hi>making a Tryal of him,</ns0:hi> than strictly, <ns0:hi>Solliciting him to sin,</ns0:hi> they came (as appeareth by their <ns0:hi>Que<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stion</ns0:hi>) to <ns0:hi>make</ns0:hi> a <ns0:hi>Tryal,</ns0:hi> whether they could intrap him, and ge<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> any Determination from him of a point, for which they might accuse him. The <ns0:hi>Question</ns0:hi> they propound to him is: <ns0:hi>Whether it be Lawful for a Man to put away his Wife for every Cause?</ns0:hi> The Word here translated <ns0:hi>Cause</ns0:hi>; signifieth not <ns0:hi>Cause,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Occasion,</ns0:hi> but <ns0:hi>Crime</ns0:hi> also. So it may be translated <ns0:hi>Crime,</ns0:hi> but they did not only put away their Wives for Crimes, but upon any occasion, in abuse of that Text. <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 24.1. <ns0:hi>When a Man hath taken a Wife and Married her, and it come to pass that she find no Favour in his Eyes, because he hath found some uncleanness in her:</ns0:hi> Which the <ns0:hi>Pharisees</ns0:hi> had interpreted, of any kind of Deformity<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> or na<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tural Infirmity, not meerly of Moral uncleanness. Had our Saviour now answered, <ns0:hi>Yes,</ns0:hi> he had Contradicted what he had formerly delivered, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 5.32. had he denied, they had Trapped him as Contradicting the Law of <ns0:hi>Moses, Deut.</ns0:hi> 24.1. (accord<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing to their Interpretation of it) So they had had whereof to accuse him.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>

ye not read, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Gen. 5.2. Mal. 2.15.</ns0:note> that he who made <ns0:hi>them</ns0:hi> at the be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ginning, made them male and female.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="5">5 And said, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Eph. 5.31.</ns0:note> For this cause, shall a man leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife, and they twain shall be one <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">

                  </ns0:gap>lesh.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="6">
                  <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Cor. 6.16.</ns0:note>6 Wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh, What therefore God hath joyned toge<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther let no man put asunder.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Mark Ch.</ns0:hi> 10.2, 3, 4. giveth us the same History of this Discourse, differing a little in the Order of the Words; but nothing as to the substance of his Discourse. Our Saviour an<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />swereth neither <ns0:hi>Yea</ns0:hi> nor <ns0:hi>Nay</ns0:hi> to their Discourse<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> but gives them a fair occasion to answer themselves, and Tacitly char<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />geth them with <ns0:hi>Ignorance,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Corruption</ns0:hi> of the Law of God. He re<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>erreth them to the first <ns0:hi>Institution of Marriage,</ns0:hi> and for that to the Book of <ns0:hi>Genesis, Ch.</ns0:hi> 1.27. <ns0:hi>&</ns0:hi> 2.24. It is as much as if our Lord had said: You own the Book of <ns0:hi>Ge<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nesis,</ns0:hi> as well as the Book of <ns0:hi>Deutronomy.</ns0:hi> In the Book of <ns0:hi>Genesis,</ns0:hi> you read the first Institution of Marriage, it was instituted by God himself; he made <ns0:hi>Male and Female, Gen.</ns0:hi> 1.27. he made the Law of Marriage, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 2.24. that a <ns0:hi>Man should leave his Father and Mother, and cleave to his Wife, and they should be one Flesh,</ns0:hi> from whence he concludeth that the Man and Wife are <ns0:hi>one Flesh</ns0:hi> in Gods Account; from hence he leaves them to conclude, whether it was probable, that <ns0:hi>Moses,</ns0:hi> whom they so reverenced, and who was so Faithful in the House of God, as a Servant, would License them to put asunder, whom God had put together: Or, whether they had not put an Interpretation upon the Law of <ns0:hi>Moses,</ns0:hi> which it could not bear, in Consistency with the Law of God. For the Sense of those Words, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 1.27. <ns0:hi>& Ch.</ns0:hi> 2.24. See the Notes on those places.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="7">7 They say unto him, Why did Moses then <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Deut. 24.1<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> Chap. 5.31.</ns0:note> command to give a writing of divorce, and to put her away?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="8">8 He saith unto them, Moses, because of the hardness of your hearts, suffered you to put away your wives: but from the beginning it was not so.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> reports this a little differently, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 10.3. As if Christ had first said unto them. <ns0:hi>What did Moses command you? And they said Moses suffered to write a Bill of Di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vorcement, and to send her away. And Iesus answered, and said. For the hardness of your Heart, he wrote you this Precept,</ns0:hi> &c. The substance of our Saviours answer seemeth to be this. <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> gave you no <ns0:hi>positive Command</ns0:hi> in the Case, he could not make a Law directly opposite to the Law of my Father. But <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> saw the <ns0:hi>Wantonness,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Wickedness</ns0:hi> of your Hearts, that you would turn away your Wives without any just and warrantable Cause, and to restrain your Extravagancies, of Cruelty to your Wives, or disorderly turning them off upon any occasion; he made a Law that <ns0:hi>none should put away his Wife, but upon a Legal Cog<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nizance of the Cause, and giving her a Bill of Divorce.</ns0:hi> Indeed possibly this <ns0:hi>Bill of Divorce</ns0:hi> was sometimes judicially granted upon irregular Causes, and <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> might connive at it, for the preventing of greater Evils, because you were always an hard Hearted, and Stiff-necked people; and you by your Tra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ditions have expounded that Law, beyond <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> his Intention, and made a Bill of Divorce grantable in Cases which he never thought of, nor intended in that Law. But the measures of Lawfulness, are neither to be taken from <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> his Tempo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rary Toleration and <ns0:hi>Connivence,</ns0:hi> nor much less from your <ns0:hi>Traditions,</ns0:hi> and Expositions of the Law of <ns0:hi>Moses,</ns0:hi> but from the <ns0:hi>Original Institution of Marriage,</ns0:hi> and from Gods <ns0:hi>Ori<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ginal Law</ns0:hi> relating to it; now God at first made but <ns0:hi>one Woman for one Man,</ns0:hi> and so united them, that he stiled them <ns0:hi>one Flesh</ns0:hi>: So as he, who puts away his Wife, doth as twere divide, and tear his own Flesh piece from piece, which is Bar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />barous, Inhumane, and unnatural. And the Law of God was not, that a Man should forsake his Wife, when ever he had a mind to it, but that he should rather forsake <ns0:hi>his Father and Mother</ns0:hi> than his Wife, that he should <ns0:hi>cleave to his Wife</ns0:hi> li<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ving, and dwelling with her, as a Man of knowledge, not ha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ting his own Flesh, Loving his Wife, <ns0:hi>as his own Body, Lo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ving and Cherishing her, Eph.</ns0:hi> 5.28.29. Now how can this possibly consist with a Mans putting away his Wife, upon every little and trivial Cause of Offence, or dislike unto her.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="9">9 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Cor. 7.10.11.</ns0:note> And I say unto you, Whosoever shall put away his wife, except <ns0:hi>it be</ns0:hi> for fornication, and shall marry another, committeth adultery: and who so marrieth her that is put away, doth com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mit adultery.<ns0:note place="bottom">We met with the like Determination of our Lords upon this Question, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 5.32. only there it was [instead of <ns0:hi>com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mitteth Adultery</ns0:hi>] <ns0:hi>causeth her to commit Adultery,</ns0:hi> that is in Case she Married again: Here our Lord saith, the like of the Husband, we have the same, <ns0:hi>Mar.</ns0:hi> 10, 11. <ns0:hi>Luk.</ns0:hi> 16.18. The reason is this, because nothing but <ns0:hi>Adultery</ns0:hi> dissolveth the Knot, and band of Marriage. Tho they be thus illegally se<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />parated, yet according to the Law of God, they are still <ns0:hi>Man</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Wife</ns0:hi>: Some have upon these Words made a Question, whether it be Lawful for the Husband, or the Wife separated for Adultery, to Marry again while each other Liveth: As to the party offending, it may be a Question, but as to the inno<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cent Person offended, it is no Question, for the <ns0:hi>Adultery</ns0:hi> of the Person offending, hath dissolved the <ns0:hi>Knot of Marriage</ns0:hi> by the Divine Law. It is true, that the Knot cannot be dissolved, without the Freedom of both Persons, each from another, but yet it seemeth against Reason, that both Persons should have the like Liberty to a second Marriage. For, 1. The <ns0:hi>Adulte<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ress,</ns0:hi> is by Gods Law a <ns0:hi>dead Woman,</ns0:hi> and so in no Capacity to a second Marriage. 2. It is unreasonable that she should make an Advantage of her own sin, and Error. 3. This might be the occasion of Adultery, to give a wicked Person a legal Liberty to satisfie an Extravagant Lust. But for the innocent Person, it is as unreasonable, that he or she should be punished for the sin of another. But what our Saviour saith here, and in the other parallel Texts, is undoubtedly to be understood, of Hus<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bands, and Wives, put away not for <ns0:hi>Adultery,</ns0:hi> but for other light and trivial Causes, for which by the Law of God no Di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vorce is allowed.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="10">10 His discples say unto him, If the case of the man be so with <ns0:hi>his</ns0:hi> wife, It is not good to marry.<ns0:note place="bottom">This is a very strange Saying, and discovers us, both the imperfect state of Christ's Disciples, and also the Tyranny of a sinful Practice grown up into a Custom. The <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> had assumed a Liberty of turning their Wives out of Doors, up<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on every light and trivial Offence, or dislike, the Disciples think; if this Licentiousness may not be allowed, it is not good to Marry. So an Holy Institution of God ordained for the Pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pagation of mankind, for the restraint of Extravagant Lust, and for the Solace and Comfort of Mans Life, should be despi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sed, rather than those unquiet Lusts, and Corruptions mor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tified, the Mortification of which, would have made those irre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gular Separations both needless, and undesirable. Surely they should rather have said: <ns0:hi>If the Case of a Man be so with his Wife then both Husbands and Wives, had need to learn to deny themselves, to comply each with another,</ns0:hi> to silence their Brutish, and boisterous Passions, that being the same Flesh, they might also have one and the same Spirit, and not be like a diseased piece of Flesh, where Humours so Quarrel, that one piece need be cut off to preserve the other. But the best of Men have their Infirmities, and as the <ns0:hi>Hebrews</ns0:hi> said, <ns0:hi>Spiritus dei non semper tangit corda prophetarum.</ns0:hi> The Spirit of God was not always upon the Hearts of the Prophets. So it is as true, <ns0:hi>Spiritus Dei, non semper & ubi<ns0:expan>
                           <ns0:am>
                              <ns0:g ref="char:abque" />
                           </ns0:am>
                           <ns0:ex>que</ns0:ex>
                        </ns0:expan> tangit cor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />da fidelium.</ns0:hi> All that the Saints say is not Gospel. Their flesh hath its turn to speak, as well as the Spirit in them. A sin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ful Liberty conceded, indulged, or <ns0:hi>connived</ns0:hi> at, by the Laws, or by the Rulers of a Church, or Place where we Live, for a long time, is not easily restrained, and even good Men may for a time be carried away with the Error of it, so as they can<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />not discern it, be Convinced of it, or be brought clearly of it to a Conformity to the Will of God.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="11">11 But he said unto them, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Cor. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">

                     </ns0:gap>.<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">

                     <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>7.9.17.</ns0:note> All men can<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />not receive this saying, save <ns0:hi>they</ns0:hi> to whom it is given.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">12 For there are some eunuchs, which were so born from <ns0:hi>their</ns0:hi> mothers womb, And there are some eunuchs, which were made eunuchs of men: And there be <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Cor. 7.<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>.34. <ns0:hi>&</ns0:hi> 9.5.15.</ns0:note> eunuchs which have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven sake, He that is able to receive <ns0:hi>it,</ns0:hi> let him re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceive <ns0:hi>it.</ns0:hi>
                  <ns0:note place="bottom">Our Saviour knowing the sinful Custom, and Practice of the Jewish Nation now for many years, and giving some allowance for that, and his Disciples infirmities, so he doth not answer them severely, as what they said might deserve, but reproves them gently; what he saith amounts to thus much, you do not consider what you say. <ns0:hi>All men</ns0:hi> without sinning against God, cannot abstain from Marriage. An Ability to live chastly without the use of Marriage, is a peculiar Gift of God, and your saying hath no place in Persons, to whom God hath not given that Gift, <ns0:hi>For it is better to Marry than to Burn.</ns0:hi> There are some whom God by Nature hath made unfit for Marriage. There are others whom Men (wickedly) make unfit for it, that they may gratifie their own Jealousie. (Thus several Courtiers were made <ns0:hi>Eunuchs,</ns0:hi> and so betrusted with the Care of Princes Wives and Concubines.) And there are some who have made themselves <ns0:hi>Eunuchs</ns0:hi> (not castrating themselves, that is wickedness) but abstaining from <ns0:hi>Marriage,</ns0:hi> and yet living Chastly (having mortified their Lusts, and brought under their Body) that they might be less incumbred with the Cares of the World, and be more free for the work of the Ministry, or be able more to give up themselves to an Holy Life and spiritual Conversation. But God, who by his Ordinance of Marriage designed to People, and continue the World, hath given to Persons different Tempers and Constitutions: So as possibly the most of Men and Women, cannot without making use of Marriage govern their Lusts. As to these, Marriage is not a matter of Choice and Deliberation, and they may, and ought to use it as an appointment of God, for the ends for which he hath instituted it. If there be any who can <ns0:hi>receive this Saying,</ns0:hi> who can without Marriage bridle his Lust, and so live in a solute and single state, as not to sin against God, by any Extravagancy of Lusts, and impure Desires and Affections, and desire, and shall do so, that he may be more spiritual, and serve God with less distraction, and be a more fit Instrument to promove the Kingdom of God in the World, let him do it.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="13">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:253" />13 Then were there brought unto him little children, that he should put <ns0:hi>his</ns0:hi> hands on them and pray, and the disciples rebuked them.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> saith, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 10.13. and <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> saith, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 18.15. they were brought <ns0:hi>that he should Touch them.</ns0:hi> A doubt may from this Text arise in the Readers mind, for what purpose the Parents, or Nurses did bring these young Children to Christ. It was not for <ns0:hi>Baptism,</ns0:hi> for he Baptized none himself, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 4.2. It is not like it was for <ns0:hi>Healing,</ns0:hi> for tho our Saviour in such Cases did sometimes <ns0:hi>Touch,</ns0:hi> or lay his Hand upon the sick Persons; yet it is not likely, that in that Case the Disci<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ples would have rebuked them, knowing that their Master used to heal such as were brought to him. It must therefore unquestionably be, that he might <ns0:hi>Bless them, Matthew</ns0:hi> here saith that he might put his Hands on them and pray. The putting of Hands upon Persons, when they <ns0:hi>Bles<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sed them,</ns0:hi> or Prayed for a Blessing on Persons, was a very usual Rite and Custom amongst the <ns0:hi>Iews. Without all Contra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />diction</ns0:hi> (saith the Apostle, <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 7.7. <ns0:hi>The lesser was Blessed of the greater.</ns0:hi>) It was a Custom amongst the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> to bring Persons, to those whom they lookt upon as Excelling in Holi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness, to be blessed and commended to God by their Prayers, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 27.4, <ns0:hi>&</ns0:hi> 48.14. The Parents, or Nurses of these Children by this Act declared, that they looked upon Christ as some great <ns0:hi>Prophet,</ns0:hi> in Favour with God; and whose <ns0:hi>Pray<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ers</ns0:hi> could prevail with God, and whose <ns0:hi>Blessing</ns0:hi> was conside<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rable as to these little ones. The <ns0:hi>Disciples rebuked them</ns0:hi>: as thinking they were too troublesome to their Ma<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>er, and not understanding what Children in Health had to do with their Master, nor perhaps having before seen such a President.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="14">14 But Jesus said, Suffer little children and forbid them not to come unto me: For of such is the kingdom of heaven.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="15">15 And he laid <ns0:hi>his</ns0:hi> hands on them, and de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />parted thence.<ns0:note place="bottom">Both <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Luke,</ns0:hi> add something to this Story. <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> saith, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 10.14. <ns0:hi>When Iesus saw it, he was much displeased, and said, Suffer the little Children to come to me, and for<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bid them not; for of such is the Kingdom of God: Verily I say unto you, whosoever shall not receive the Kingdom of God, as a little Child, he shall not enter therein. And he took them up in his Arms, put his Hands upon them and Blessed them. Luke</ns0:hi> saith the same, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 18.15. only he saith. He called them unto him, and leaves out what <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> hath, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 16. of <ns0:hi>Christ taking them up in his Arms, putting his Hands upon them, and Blessing them.</ns0:hi> From this Text, Di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vines will prove the <ns0:hi>Baptism of Children,</ns0:hi> because <ns0:hi>theirs is the Kingdom of Heaven</ns0:hi>; which whether we understand of the <ns0:hi>Church,</ns0:hi> and the Dispensation of the Grace of Christ under the Gospel, viz. That the Gospel-Church is made up of In<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fants, as well as more adult Persons, or that the Grace of Christ under the Gospel, viz. <ns0:hi>Remission of sins</ns0:hi> through the Blood of Christ, doth belong to some Children, as well as to grown Persons: Or, of the <ns0:hi>Kingdom of Glory,</ns0:hi> viz. <ns0:hi>Children</ns0:hi> shall go to Heaven, as well as grown Persons. The Argument is well drawn from this Text: Those who have a right to a Member-ship in the Church, are to be Baptized: Or, those who have a right to the Kingdom of Glory may be Baptized. But one or both of these are affirmed in this Text. We must take heed, we do not found <ns0:hi>Infant-Baptism,</ns0:hi> upon the Ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ample of Christ in this Text, for it is certain that he did not <ns0:hi>Baptise</ns0:hi> these Children, <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> only saith, he <ns0:hi>took them into his Arms, laid his Hands on them, and Blessed them.</ns0:hi> The Argument for Infant-Baptism, from this Text is founded up<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on his Words, uttered on this occasion, not upon his Pra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ctice. <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> addeth, that our Saviour told them, <ns0:hi>That un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />less a Man received the Kingdom of God as a little Child, he could not enter into it.</ns0:hi> But we opened those words before, <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 18.3. where we met with the same in Effect.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>

                     </ns0:gap>ying him at le<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">

                     </ns0:gap>t a Civil Ho<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mage, as to his Superiour) he salutes <ns0:hi>him</ns0:hi> with the ordinary Title, they gave to their <ns0:hi>Teachers</ns0:hi>: Master, <ns0:hi>Good Master,</ns0:hi> he propoundeth a <ns0:hi>Grave Question to him,</ns0:hi> what he should do that he might get to Heaven<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> But yet, he doth not propound<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> the Question in those terms; but, <ns0:hi>What good thing should I do, that I may have Eternal Life?</ns0:hi> It appeareth, by his respe<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>t shewed to Christ at his coming, and by the Question propo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sed, and by his going <ns0:hi>away sorrowful,</ns0:hi> when our Saviours An<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />swer did not satisfie him, that he did not come upon any C<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>p<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tio<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>s design to entrap our Saviour, but out of a Desire to learn; but yet, it appeareth plainly, that he was a <ns0:hi>Pharisee,</ns0:hi> or a Disciple of the <ns0:hi>Pharisees,</ns0:hi> and though his Life was in his own Hands, that he had a Power in himself to do so<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>e good thing, by which he might merit Eternal Life, or upon the doing of which, he might at least obtain Everlasting Life; tho not as a strict reward for his Work, without any Con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sideration of a <ns0:hi>Messias</ns0:hi>: He grants an <ns0:hi>Eternal state,</ns0:hi> he de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />clares his Desire of an Eternal Happiness, he declareth his Rea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />diness to do some <ns0:hi>Good thing,</ns0:hi> that he might obtain it.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="17">17 And he said unto him, Why callest thou me good? There <ns0:hi>is none</ns0:hi> good but one, * <ns0:hi>that is</ns0:hi> God: But if thou wilt enter into life keep the commandements.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> omitteth the latter Clause, and only saith, <ns0:hi>Thou know<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />est the Commandements</ns0:hi>: So saith <ns0:hi>Luke, Ch.</ns0:hi> 18. <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 19, 20. Our Saviours design here was, not to shew this young Man by this Answer, the way by which it was possible, that he or any other might come to Heaven, but only to convince him of the Er<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rors of the Pharasaical Doctrine; they would not own Christ to be God, nor to be come forth from God, They taught Eternal Life to be obtainable by the Works of the Law<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> and by a fulfilling of the Law, according to that imperfect Sense which they gave of it, of which we heard much, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 5. Now (saith our Saviour.) Seeing you will not own me to be God, nor yet to have come from God, why callest thou me good? There is none Originally, E<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>sentially, and absolutely good, but God: There is none Derivatively good, but he deriveth his Goodness from God. How callest thou me Good, whom thou wilt neither own to be God, nor to derive from God? <ns0:hi>But if thou wilt enter into Life, keep the Commandements.</ns0:hi> This was the Doctrine of the <ns0:hi>Pharisees</ns0:hi>: That men might keep the Commandements. Saith our Saviour, the way to Eternal Life according to your Doctrine, is plain before thee: You say, Men may perfectly keep the Commandements of God. He that doth so shall be saved. Therefore <ns0:hi>keep the Commandements</ns0:hi>: Not that our Saviour thought he could do it<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>or that there did lye a passable Road to Heaven, that way, bu<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> that he might convince him of his Error, and the need he had <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> a Saviour.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="18">18 He saith unto him, Which? Jesus said, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Exod. 20.13. Deut. 5.17.</ns0:note> Thou shalt do no murder, Thou shalt not com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mit adultery, thou shalt not steal, Thou shalt not bear false witness.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="19">19 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 15.4.</ns0:note> Honour thy Father, and <ns0:hi>thy</ns0:hi> Mother<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                  <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Lev. 19.18. Chap. 22.39. Rom. 13.9. Gal. 5.14. Jam. 2.8.</ns0:note> Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thy self.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> addeth: <ns0:hi>Defraud not, Ch.</ns0:hi> 10.19. but <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> doth not put in, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 18.20. Three things we may observe. 1. There are no Commandements mentioned, but those of the second Table. 2. Nor are they reckoned up in Order. 3. The tenth Commandement is expressed by: <ns0:hi>Thou shalt Love thy Neigh<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bour as thy self</ns0:hi>: Which elsewhere our Saviour calls the second great Commandement, and makes Comprehensive of all the Commandements of the second Table. We must not from our Saviours order here, in the Enumeration of the Comman<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dements, either conclude, that the Precepts of the second Ta<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ble, are greater than those of the first, or that it is enough to keep them, in order to Eternal Life: Nor yet, that the fifth Commandement is lesser than the sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, because it is put after them. But, 1. Our Saviour had re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ckoned up Commandements enough to convince this Man, that he could not by keeping the Commandements hope for Eternal Life. 2. He had reckoned those by some, of which he intended by and by to convince him, that he had not kept the Commandements. 3. And those of the Non-Observation, of which it was most easie to convince him. 4. The <ns0:hi>Pharisees</ns0:hi> lookt upon these, as the most Vulgar and easie Commandements. 5. Because Love to our Neighbour, is an excellent Evidence of our Love to God. As concerning the Order, in which they are Enumerated: It was not our Saviours business here to shew which was the greatest Commandement, that he hath else<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />where determined; calling, <ns0:hi>Thou shalt Love the Lord thy God with all thy Heart,</ns0:hi> &c. the first and great Commande<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment, here he is not Sollicitous about the Order.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="20">20 The young man saith unto him, All these things have I kept from my youth up, what lack I yet?<ns0:note place="bottom">Those words, <ns0:hi>What lack I yet?</ns0:hi> Are no<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> in <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Luke.</ns0:hi> The young Man understood <ns0:hi>these Commandements,</ns0:hi> accord<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing to the <ns0:hi>Pharisees</ns0:hi> Interpretation of them, who as we heard, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 5. interpreted them only as prohibiting the Overt-Acts, not the inward Lusts<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> and Motions of the Heart, together with the means, or occasions leading to such Acts. <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> saith, <ns0:hi>He had not known Lust, if the Law had not said, Thou shalt not Covet, Rom.</ns0:hi> 7.7. Men that deceive themselves with false Glosses, and Interpretations may think they keep the Commandements of God<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> and be very confident of a Righte<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ousness in themselves. But it is impo<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>sible others should be so: <ns0:hi>What l<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ck I yet?</ns0:hi> He expected Christ should have set him some new Task<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> and was not aware, that he only wanted a bet<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter knowledge and understanding of the Law, to convince him of his mistake.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="21">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:254" />21 Jesus saith unto him, If thou wilt be per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fect <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 6.20. Luk. 12.33. <ns0:hi>&</ns0:hi> 16.9. 1 Tim. 6.18, 19.</ns0:note> Go, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> sell that thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven, and come, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> follow me.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> repeats it thus, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 10.21. <ns0:hi>Then Iesus beholding him, loved him. And said unto him, One thing thou lackest. Go thy way, sell, whatsoever thou hast and give to the Poor, and thou shalt have Treasure in Heaven, and come, take up thy Cross, and follow me. Luk. ch.</ns0:hi> 18.22. repeats it as <ns0:hi>Matthew,</ns0:hi> only <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>e begins it with, <ns0:hi>One thing thou lackest<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> Mark</ns0:hi> saith, that <ns0:hi>Iesus beholding him loved him,</ns0:hi> not with a special saving Love, for he sent him away sad, upon his going, he tells his Disc<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ples, that it was a very hard thing for a Rich man to come to Heaven, he tells him, One thing was want<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing to him; but he loved him with such a common Love, as he loveth all his Creatures with, and more especially, such as are better than others All that can be concluded from hence is: <ns0:hi>Th<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                           <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> Acts of moral Righteousness are pleasing to God.</ns0:hi> He saith to him, <ns0:hi>If thou wilt be perfect</ns0:hi>: That is, in keeping the Commandements of God. The <ns0:hi>Papist</ns0:hi> make a great deal of stir to found upon this Text, their <ns0:hi>Councels of Perfection.</ns0:hi> As if Christ here were advising only the young Man, to do something beyond what the Law strictly required, in Order to a more perfect state than others. But that this cannot be the Sense of the Words will appear to him, who will diligently consider, 1. That this had been need<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />less for our Saviour, for directing the young Man to keep the Commandements, in Order to his obtaining Everlasting Life, had sufficiently declared, that the keeping o<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> the Commande<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ments was Perfection enough. 2. He says, One thing is want<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ing to thee: That is, in Order to thy obtaining Everlasting Life, which had not been true, if our Saviour had granted him to have <ns0:hi>kept all the Commandements,</ns0:hi> for he had before let him know, that the keeping them was sufficient. Our Saviour therefore, by this Speech only indeavours to convince him, that he had not <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> all the Commandements. But it may be ob<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />jected, <ns0:hi>How <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                           <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ould that be? For there was no Commande<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment that <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> him to go sell all that he had, and give to the Poor:</ns0:hi> I answer: There was a Commandement, <ns0:hi>That he should Love the Lord his God with all his Heart, and Soul, and Strength,</ns0:hi> which he could not do, unless he had an Heart ready to obey any Command God should lay upon him, which our Saviour puts upon the Tryal, by this <ns0:hi>special Precept.</ns0:hi> 2. There was a Commandement, that <ns0:hi>he should Love his Neigh<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bour as himself,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>that he should not Covet.</ns0:hi> Now not to be ready at the Commandement of God, liberally to relieve the poor Members of Christ, argued a <ns0:hi>Covetous mind</ns0:hi>; more in Love with his Estate, than with God: So as though this was not before specially Commanded, yet it was Commanded ge<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nerally, and that he would have understood, had he rightly understood the Law of God; especially, having such a Promise annexed, as <ns0:hi>thou shalt have Treasure in Heaven.</ns0:hi> 3. Nor must all the Command be taken to be included in those Words, <ns0:hi>Go sell all that thou hast, and give to the Poor,</ns0:hi> but the follow<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing Words must also be taken in. <ns0:hi>And come, and take up the Cross, and follow me.</ns0:hi> Perfection here, is not made to lye in a <ns0:hi>Voluntary Poverty</ns0:hi> only, but in coming after, and following of Christ with a free taking up of the Cross. In short: No man can be perfect in keeping the Commandements of God. <ns0:hi>That doth not love God with all his Heart, Soul, and Strength:</ns0:hi> Nor can any Man pretend to this, that hath not an Heart rea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dy to obey God in all things, whether more generally, or more specially Commanded. Nor can any man fulfil the Duty of the second Table<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> without first fulfilling the Duties of the first; for if our Love to our Neighbour flow not from a Love to God, it is no Act of Obedience, and Consequently no fulfilling the Law, which is not fulfilled by meer doing the external Duty of it, but by doing what is required in it, out of an Obedience unto God, which cannot be without a first lo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ving God.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="22">22 But when the young man heard that say<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing, he went away sorrowful, for he had great possessions.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> saith the same, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 10.22. So doth <ns0:hi>Luke, Ch.</ns0:hi> 18.23. He was sorry, that he had ever propounded the Question, or that the terms were such, as his covetous Heart could not com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ply with. He would have had Heaven, if he could have had it cheap: Or it may be, he would have parted with some<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thing for it, but to <ns0:hi>Sell all</ns0:hi> was an hard Saying! Or he was sorry to see himself so confuted, and convinced, that what<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />soever he Dreamed, he had not kept the Commandements, and had not an Heart prepared to obey God in one thing. It is not said, <ns0:hi>Because he loved his great Possessions,</ns0:hi> but, for he <ns0:hi>had great Possessions:</ns0:hi> Yet the first is intended. It is an hard thing for us to have a great Concern in the World, and not to love it more than God. He <ns0:hi>went away,</ns0:hi> he would hear no more of that Discourse: How many would have Heaven, if they might have it upon their own terms? How few are willing to come up to Gods terms? How false and deceitful are our Hearts? They will perswade us we have done all, when in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />deed we have done nothing, nor are prepared to do any thing in Truth and Sincerity? We are not <ns0:hi>Perfect,</ns0:hi> something is wanting to us, till <ns0:hi>To Will,</ns0:hi> to do whatsoever God requireth of us, be present with us, tho, when it comes too, we may want strength to perform.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="23">23 Then said Jesus unto his disciples, Verily I say unto you, that <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 span">
                        <ns0:desc>〈…〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 10.</ns0:note> a rich man shall hardly enter into the kingdom of heaven.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="24">24 And again I say unto you, it is easier for a Camel to go through the eye of a needle, than for a rich man to enter into the kingdom of God.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> saith, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 10.23. <ns0:hi>And Iesus looked round about, and said to his Disciples. How hardly shall they that have Riches enter into the Kingdom of God. And the Disciples were astonished at his Words, but Iesus answereth again, and saith unto them. Children! How hard is it for them that trust in Riches, to enter into the Kingdom of God? It is easier for a Camel to go through the Eye of a Needle, than for a Rich man to enter into the Kingdom of God. Luke</ns0:hi> saith, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 18.24. <ns0:hi>And when Iesus saw that he was sorrowful, he said, How hardly shall they that have Riches enter into the Kingdom of God? For it is easier for a Ca<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mel to go through a Needles Eye, than for a Rich man to enter into the Kingdom of God.</ns0:hi> Our Lord, seeing the young Man that came to him so briskly, with such a Zeal for his Soul, and appearing warmth of Desire, to be instructed in the right way to Heaven, and asking for a <ns0:hi>Task</ns0:hi> to be set him: First, what good thing he should do in Order to that end, then calling for more; when our Saviour had reckoned up some Commandements to be observed. <ns0:hi>What lack I yet,</ns0:hi> Saith he? <ns0:hi>Go away</ns0:hi> quite dampt and sorrowful, when our Saviour said not to him. <ns0:hi>Give thy Body to be burned,</ns0:hi> no nor yet, <ns0:hi>cut off a right Hand,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Foot,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>pluck out a right Eye.</ns0:hi> Only part with some of thy Circumstances, <ns0:hi>Sell what thou hast and give to the Poor.</ns0:hi> A thing he might have done, and have been a Man still perfect; both as to his Essential, and Integral parts. He hence takes occasion to Discourse with his Disciples, the danger of <ns0:hi>Riches,</ns0:hi> and the ill influence they have upon mens Souls, with Relation to their Eternal Welfare. <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> say, he spake it by way of <ns0:hi>Question.</ns0:hi> How hardly? <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> delivereth it as spoken positively. <ns0:hi>A Rich m<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>n shall hardly enter, &c.</ns0:hi> The Sense is the same, only the <ns0:hi>In<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />terrogation</ns0:hi> seems to aggravate the Difficulty, and to fortifie the <ns0:hi>Affirmation,</ns0:hi> as much as to say, A Rich man shall <ns0:hi>very hardly</ns0:hi> enter into the Kingdom of Heaven. The Disciples were <ns0:hi>astonished at this</ns0:hi> (saith <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi>) which made our Savi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />our say it over again, with a little Exposition. <ns0:hi>How hard is it for them that trust in Riches, to enter into the Kingdom of God?</ns0:hi> Which Exposition is so far from a Correction, or Abatement of the severity of his former Speech, that some Judge it rather a Confirmation of it, for he goes on with say<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing: <ns0:hi>It is easier for a Camel to go through the Eye of a Needle.</ns0:hi> But why should this <ns0:hi>astonish</ns0:hi> the Disciples, who had no reason upon this Account to <ns0:hi>Fear</ns0:hi> for themselves, who had forsaken all to follow Christ? Possibly, because it was so con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />trary to the common Opinion of the World, who did not only as in <ns0:hi>Malachys</ns0:hi> time, call the <ns0:hi>Proud Happy</ns0:hi>; but thought God had scarce any Favour for any but the Rich: In opposi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion to which Christ, <ns0:hi>Luk.</ns0:hi> 6.20.24. <ns0:hi>Blesseth the Poor,</ns0:hi> and pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nounceth Woes to the <ns0:hi>Rich,</ns0:hi> as having <ns0:hi>received their Conso<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lation.</ns0:hi> As to the Words themselves. The design of our Savi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />our in them, was not to condemn Riches, as in themselves Damnable; nor yet to deny Salvation to all <ns0:hi>Rich Persons</ns0:hi>: Our Lord knew, that <ns0:hi>Abraham, Isaac, Iacob, Iob,</ns0:hi> were all Rich Persons, and yet in Heaven, so was <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Solomon,</ns0:hi> &c. He also knew, that Riches are the Gifts of God, Good things, not in themselves Pernicious: His design was only to shew, That they are dangerous Temptations, Solliciting and entising our Hearts, into so great a Love of them, and Affecti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on to them, as is not consistent with our Duty, with reference to God; and giving the Heart of Man such Advantages for the Lusts of <ns0:hi>Pride, Coveteousness, Ambition, Oppression, Luxury,</ns0:hi> (some or other, of which are Predominate in all Souls) that it is very hard for a Rich man, so far to deny himself, as to do what he must do, if ever he will be saved. For those words in <ns0:hi>Mark, Them that trust in Riche.</ns0:hi> I take them ra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther, to give the reason of the Difficulty, than to be an Abate<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment of what he had before said. For to <ns0:hi>trust in Riches,</ns0:hi> is to place an Happiness in them, to Promise our selves a security from them, so as to be careless of a further H<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ppiness<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                     <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 49.6. <ns0:hi>&</ns0:hi> 52.7. 1 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 6.17. That which makes it so hard for a Rich man to be saved, is the Difficulty of having <ns0:hi>Riches,</ns0:hi> and not placing our <ns0:hi>Felicity</ns0:hi> in them, being secure; because of them, and having our Hearts cleave unto them, so as we can<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />not deny our selves in them, to obey any Command of God: And the suffering them to be Temptations to us, to <ns0:hi>Pride, Luxury, Ambition, Oppression, Contempt,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Despising of others, Coveteousness, &c.</ns0:hi> Upon these Accounts our Saviour goeth on and saith. <ns0:hi>It is easier for a Camel to go through the Eye of a Needle, than for a Rich man to enter into the Kingdom of God.</ns0:hi> Which doubtless was a <ns0:hi>Proverbial Expressi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on</ns0:hi> in use, then amongst the <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> to signifie a thing of great Difficulty, by terms importing impo<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>sibility: Or, else the Phrase may signifie an impossibility, without the extraordi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nary influence of Divine Grace, as our Saviour seemeth to ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pound it in the next Verses.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="25">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:254" />25 When his disciples heard <ns0:hi>it,</ns0:hi> they were ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceedingly amazed, saying, who then can be sa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ved?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="26">26 But Jesus beheld them, and said unto them, With men this is impossible, but <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Jer. 32.17. Zech. 8.6. Luk. 1.37. <ns0:hi>&</ns0:hi> 18.27.</ns0:note> with God all things are possible.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> saith, <ns0:hi>They were astonished out of Measure saying among themselves, &c.</ns0:hi> All three Evangelists agree in the same substance of the other Words. But why are the Disci<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ples amazed? Or, why do they say, who then can be saved? Are there not in all places more Poor than Rich Persons: The Disciples might reasonably conclude, that Poor Persons were by their Poverty also exposed to many great and dangerous Temptations, that even they, tho they had not Riches, yet might too much place Felicity in them, and Covet what they had not; and from hence Collect a Difficulty for any to get to Heaven. Our Saviour saith unto them, <ns0:hi>With men this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.</ns0:hi> If men indeed were left all to themselves, none would be saved, the Black-a-Moor cannot change his skin, nor the <ns0:hi>Leopard his Spots.</ns0:hi> But God can bring men to Heaven, by the mighty Power of his Grace, he can change a Rich mans Heart, and take it off from too much Love of Riches, and make him to despise and contemn his Wealth, and to put his Trust in the living God: Or, a Poor mans Heart, and make him also Poor in Spirit, and Rich in Grace.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="27">27 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mar. 10.28. Luk. 18.28.</ns0:note> Then answered Peter, and said unto him, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 4.20. Luk. 5.11.</ns0:note> Behold we have forsaken all, and followed thee, what shall we have therefore?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="28">28 And Jesus said unto them, Verily I say un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to you, That ye which have followed me in the regeneration, when the Son of man shall sit in the throne of his glory, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Luk. 22.28, 29, 30.</ns0:note> ye also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> repeateth the Words of <ns0:hi>Peter</ns0:hi> in part, but neither of them have this part of our Lords answer, par<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ticularly respecting his Apostles. We heard before, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 4.18.21. of <ns0:hi>Peter,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Andrew,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Iames,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Iohns forsaking all,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>following of Christ,</ns0:hi> when he called them, the others doubt<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ss did the same: <ns0:hi>Peter</ns0:hi> observing, that our Saviour laid not the stress of Mens Salvation, either upon Riches, or Poverty, but upon the Frame of Mens Spirits, their Humility, Self-denyal, their Obedience to, and readiness to follow him; re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />joyneth these Words, and saith, <ns0:hi>We have forsaken all, and followed thee, what shall we have?</ns0:hi> Some think, that he had an Expectation of something in this Life, according to the Notion which the other <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> had, and it is Apparant, the Dis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ciples had some Tincture of a secular Kingdom, which the <ns0:hi>Messias</ns0:hi> should Exercise. But considering our Lords former Discourse, could not be so interpreted, and the Disciples question, <ns0:hi>Who then can be saved?</ns0:hi> I cannot agree that. And for the same reason I cannot agree, that <ns0:hi>the coming of the Son of Man in his Glory,</ns0:hi> mentioned <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 28. should be un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />derstood of his coming in his <ns0:hi>Mediatory Kingdom,</ns0:hi> (as some would have it) but of his last coming, which is most properly called, <ns0:hi>The coming of the Son of Man in his Glory,</ns0:hi> mentioned, 1 <ns0:hi>Thes.</ns0:hi> 4.15, 16, 17. <ns0:hi>Iud. &</ns0:hi> 14. and that the thing here Promised to the Apostles, is not a preference in the Church, but a further Degree of Honour, and Glory in the Day of Judgment. <ns0:hi>You which have followed me in the Regenera<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion</ns0:hi>: That is at this time, while I have been by my Do<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ctrine <ns0:hi>Reforming</ns0:hi> the World. In the <ns0:hi>Regeneration</ns0:hi> of my Church, while I have been putting it into a new State. Some make those Words, <ns0:hi>In the Regeneration,</ns0:hi> to refer to the next Words. <ns0:hi>In the Regeneration</ns0:hi>: That is, <ns0:hi>In the day of Iudg<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment,</ns0:hi> when Christ shall come in his Glory. The Apostle in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />deed, <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 3.21. calleth that day, <ns0:hi>The time of the Restitution of all things.</ns0:hi> And the Prophet speaks of it, as the time of the <ns0:hi>New Heavens,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>New Earth, Is.</ns0:hi> 66.22. So doth the A<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />postle, 2 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 3.13. and <ns0:hi>Iohn,</ns0:hi> in <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 21.1. It is not much material, to which part we apply the term. <ns0:hi>You that have followed me:</ns0:hi> That is, who have followed, and shall go on and follow me, for this Promise cannot belong to <ns0:hi>Iudas</ns0:hi> the Son of Perdition: <ns0:hi>You shall sit upon twelve Thrones. Iudges and Princes</ns0:hi> use to have <ns0:hi>Assessors,</ns0:hi> that sit with them in Judgment. He mentions <ns0:hi>twelve Thrones,</ns0:hi> because he had now twelve Disciples, his Apostles, and tho afterward <ns0:hi>Iudas</ns0:hi> fell away, yet <ns0:hi>Mathias</ns0:hi> succeeded, <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 1.26. So as the twelve Thrones shall not be empty; but filled up with twelve that followed Christ (for such a one was <ns0:hi>Mathias<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> Acts</ns0:hi> 1.21.) <ns0:hi>Iudging the twelve Tribes of Israel.</ns0:hi> Tho the Tribes were thirteen, yet they usually went under the Notion of twelve, because <ns0:hi>Levi</ns0:hi> was not counted, as having no particular Pos<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />session: That is, judging the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> for their Unbelief, and not reception of me: Judging others also<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> but Judgment shall begin at the House of God. Doubtless this Promise imports, that the Apostles shall have a higher place in Glory at the great Day than ordinary Believers: yet the Apostle saith <ns0:hi>the Saints shall Iudge the World,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 6.2.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
